questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of worsening myalgia, restlessness, and sweating. Her jaw had been feeling tight for 2 days, and she felt unable to walk properly due to stiffness. She was a keen gardener. She had a history of hypertension, depression, and gastro-oesophageal reflux. She was taking bendroflumethiazide, sertraline, and ranitidine. On examination she was sitting straight up in bed. Her blood pressure was 138/76 mmHg and her heart rate was 102 beats/minute. She was orientated to time, place, and person. Her face was taut with a wide smile and tense masseters. She was sweating profusely. She had dilated but reactive pupils. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Her skin was intact except for a 6 cm healing laceration along her right shin. Neurologic exam: Diffusely increased tone and rigidity in all muscle groups. Occasional twitches visible. Muscle power 5/5; reflexes brisk but equal; gag reflex elicited a bite. Sensation intact.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tetanus Tetanus is the most likely diagnosis due to risk factors (gender and age mean she is unlikely to have completed a vaccination course; gardening injuries are a recognized route of entry) and to the clinical features of excessive muscle spasm and sympathetic activity. Generalized tetanus is commonly a descending pattern after a nonspecific prodrome of fever, malaise, and headache. Patients are usually cognitively intact. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is most commonly associated with drugs affecting dopamine activity, within 1–4 weeks of initiating or changing dose; it is also usually associated with an altered mental status. She has had no history of exposure to rabies, nor are the classic clinical features of rabies present, such as hydrophobia or insomnia. She has no features of cognitive impairment or confusion that would be expected with a herpes encephalitis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q12

questions.stem: A 37-year-old construction worker presented to the emergency department with fever and painful muscle spasms for 1 day. On examination, his temperature is 38.1°C, pulse 122 beats/minute, blood pressure 135/80 mmHg, and he has a small wound on his hand with surrounding erythema and induration that he says he sustained because of puncturing his hand with a nail.
questions.lead_in: What is the first-line antimicrobial of choice to inhibit further toxin production contributing to his illness?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole Treatment with metronidazole, along with tetanus immune globulin, should be administered. Metronidazole is recommended as first-line antimicrobial therapy for tetanus. The other antibiotics listed are recommended as second-line agents.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q36

questions.question: Tetanus

parts.text: Why and how does it cause paralysis

questions.model_answer:
a) Bacteria/toxin: Clostridium tetani, produces tetanospasmin (also tetanolysin, of unclear clinical significance).
b) Mechanism of paralysis/rigidity: toxin enters at the neuromuscular junction, undergoes retrograde axonal transport to motor neuron cell bodies in the brainstem/spinal cord, then diffuses to presynaptic terminals of inhibitory glycinergic interneurons and GABAergic neurons. It cleaves synaptobrevin, blocking release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine, GABA). Loss of this inhibition raises resting motor neuron firing and removes limits on reflex responses to afferent stimuli, producing sustained muscular rigidity and spasms (not flaccid paralysis — it is disinhibition, causing spastic contraction).
c) Four classic clinical syndromes: (1) generalized tetanus, (2) localized tetanus, (3) cephalic tetanus, (4) neonatal tetanus.
d) Management (3): (1) wound debridement plus antibiotics (metronidazole IV), (2) passive immunization with human tetanus immune globulin (HTIG) to neutralize unbound toxin, plus active immunization with tetanus toxoid, (3) benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam) to control rigidity/spasms, with supportive care/ICU management (autonomic control, ventilatory support) as needed.

parts.text: Name the bacteria and the toxin involved
Describe mechanism of action for toxin

cohort_answer.text: Bacteria/toxin: Clostridium tetani; Tetanospasmin (Tetanus Toxin). MOA: Tetanus toxin binds to the presynaptic inhibitory interneuron of the neuromuscular junction and prevents GABA release that would send inhibitory impulses to the motorneuron, thus preventing muscle relaxation. Syndromes: Generalized; Local; Cephalic; Neonatal. Treatment: Administer Human Tetanus Immune globulin at the wound site; Provide Tetanus Immunization at a different site; Provide Antibiotics for 7-10 days (Metronidazole IV preferred)

questions.question: You see a 6 year-old child presenting following a cat bite, who he was playing “aggressively” with. On examination, there are 2 puncture wounds on the left arm, with no surrounding erythema or edema

parts.text: Presuming no antibiotic allergies, what antibiotic should be given for prophylaxis?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he has not received any immunizations after 4 months?
Regarding tetanus management, how should the child be managed if he is HIV positive has received all of his routine immunizations except for pre-school boosters?

questions.model_answer:
a) Prophylactic antibiotic: amoxicillin-clavulanate (covers Pasteurella multocida as well as oral anaerobes/streptococci from the cat's mouth).
b) Fully immunized except for pre-school boosters (tetanus-prone puncture wound): give a Tdap (or Td) booster now, as the primary series is complete but the age-appropriate booster is overdue; tetanus immune globulin (TIG) is not needed since the primary series was completed.
c) No immunizations after 4 months of age (incomplete primary series, tetanus-prone wound): give both the age-appropriate tetanus-containing vaccine (to complete/continue the primary series) AND tetanus immune globulin (TIG), since the primary series is incomplete.
d) HIV-positive, immunized except pre-school boosters (tetanus-prone wound): give the Tdap (or Td) booster AND tetanus immune globulin (TIG) - immunocompromised patients should receive TIG for tetanus-prone wounds regardless of vaccination history, as their immune response to prior vaccination may be inadequate.
questions.beyond_mandell: ACIP/Canadian Immunization Guide tetanus prophylaxis wound management recommendations, including the immunocompromised host modification.

questions.question:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.

cohort_answer.text: Clostridium tetani. Generalized tetanus often begins with risus sardonicus and trismus ("lockjaw"). Abdominal rigidity may be present. Spasm resembles decorticate posturing with opisthotonic posturing. Patient does not lose consciousness, experiences severe pain during spasms, often triggered by sensory stimuli. Airway obstruction or diaphragm involvement can compromise respiration. Autonomic dysfunction is leading cause of death.

questions.question:

Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.

cohort_answer.text: No specific micro test - clinical dx or EMG (do not attempt to culture from wound - often false +/-). Tetanus is diagnosed clinically; laboratory testing cannot confirm or exclude the condition and is primarily useful for excluding intoxications that mimic tetanus. Attempts to culture C. tetani from wounds are not useful.

questions.question:

cohort_answer.text: Spatula test (spec 100%, sens 94%) - touch back of pharyngeal wall, reflex contraction of masseters = positive test, gag reflex is negative. EMG.

questions.question:
Q33 (2011 PM)
Patient with trismus, muscle spasms etc.

parts.text: F) Approach to treatment (early management, intermediate stage, convalescent)

cohort_answer.text: ACUTE: Airway management; muscle relaxation (benzos, sedation with propofol); neutralize toxin (human tetanus immunoglobulin IM with part of dose infiltrating wound); active immunization at 0, 4-6 weeks, 6-12 months and q10 years; stop toxin production (surgical debridement); abx (metronidazole or penicillin x 7-10 days); supportive measures; manage autonomic instability. INTERMEDIATE: complete vaccine series and continue q10 years. CONVALESCENCE: manage complications (fracture of spinal bones, rhabdo, PNA, PE, cerebral palsy in neonates)
Tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin). Two toxins, tetanospasmin and tetanolysin, are produced; tetanospasmin is encoded on a plasmid present in all toxigenic strains; tetanolysin is of uncertain importance.

Toxin enters CNS through presynaptic terminals of LMNs then to spinal cord and brainstem via retrograde axonal transport. Enters interneurons and blocks neurotransmission, net inactivation of inhibitory neurotransmission = loss of inhibition = increased muscle tone, painful spasms, widespread autonomic instability, muscle rigidity

ACUTE: Airway management; muscle relaxation; neutralize toxin (human tetanus immunoglobulin); active immunization; stop toxin production (surgical debridement); abx (metronidazole or penicillin x 7-10 days); supportive measures; manage autonomic instability. INTERMEDIATE: complete vaccine series. CONVALESCENCE: manage complications
